title: Internal vs External users: licensing tier changes available features
detail: Kiteworks licensing docs define Internal Users (customer domain) vs External Users (everyone else). All Internal Users are Licensed; External Users are Licensed only if granted edit+download+upload+manage in at least one folder (Collaborator/Manager/Owner folder roles) or can initiate email. External Users limited to view/download/upload-only are Nonlicensed. Two users with the same login flow therefore get different feature sets based on internal/external classification plus folder role.
evidence: kiteworks.com Packaging and Licensing PDF (Enterprise 8.0): 'Licensed Users: All Internal Users, plus External Users who have privileges to at least edit, download, upload, and manage all files in at least one folder (Collaborator, Manager, and Owner folder roles) or initiate an email.' / 'Nonlicensed Users: External Users who can only view, download, or upload.'

title: Same folder, different folder-role: Owner/Manager/Collaborator vs Downloader/Uploader/Viewer
detail: Per-folder roles split into two tiers: Owner, Manager, Collaborator (full: edit/download/upload/manage) vs Downloader, Uploader, Viewer (limited). Two regular users in the same folder see different actions. If an External User can upload AND download to the same folder they flip to Licensed status — a state change in the user's classification driven by folder-role assignment.
evidence: kiteworks.com Packaging and Licensing PDF folder-role table; Getting Started Guide: 'assign users the Collaborator role with permissions to edit, download, send the file, and more. Or you can assign them the Viewer role with limited permissions... Your Kiteworks administrator determines which roles you can assign.'

title: Role-based feature toggles: same role, different client access (web/mobile/SFTP)
detail: Kiteworks role-based permissions let admins enable/disable email and collaboration features per role AND enable/disable access to web, mobile, and SFTP clients per role. Two users holding the same nominal role can therefore have different client surfaces (e.g., one can use SFTP, the other web-only) depending on role configuration. Client allow-listing is per-role, not per-user.
evidence: kiteworks.com Internal Messaging Doc (FTC Safeguards): 'rolebased permissions system allows a customer to control access... based on the role of the user. A customer can enable or disable email and collaboration features for different roles, and enable access to Kiteworks web, mobile, and SFTP clients.'

title: User Profiles bundle privileges: /profiles API maps users to feature sets
detail: Admin docs describe a /profiles endpoint to manage privileges assigned to users; User Profile lists carry the features and settings for each profile. Separately, /roles exposes directory roles and /adminRoles manages administrator-role assignment (only system admins can grant admin; users cannot self-promote). Behavior differences between users are therefore driven by profile+role assignment, not just identity.
evidence: Kiteworks admin guide: 'The /profiles/ endpoint security API allows your application to manage the privileges assigned to kiteworks users... Role APIs allow you to get details about directory roles... adminRoles API allows your application to manage the assignment of administrator roles to users... Users cannot promote themselves to system administrators.'

title: Guest-type users: no personal space, uploads owned by the sharer
detail: Kiteworks (via ownCloud lineage docs) distinguishes Guest users: regular users with restricted permissions, identified by email, with NO personal space and NO file ownership — files they upload/create are owned by the sharer; quota is the sharer's quota; apps are admin-whitelisted; they deactivate when no shares remain. A guest and a full user performing the same upload end up with different ownership records.
evidence: doc.owncloud.com user_roles (ownCloud, a Kiteworks company): Guest 'Has no personal space... Has no file ownership (ownership of uploaded/created files is directed to sharer)... Quota is that of the sharer... Becomes deactivated when no shares are left.'

title: Send-files recipients: account holders vs prompted-to-register recipients
detail: When files are sent, recipients with accounts get a link; recipients without accounts are prompted to create one, and files are deleted from the server after link expiry. The same 'send' action produces different onboarding flows and different data lifetimes depending on recipient account state.
evidence: Kiteworks Getting Started Guide: 'If a recipient doesn't have a user account on the server, they'll be prompted to create one.' / 'After the link expires, the files are deleted from the server.'

title: Per-user policy variance: file-type filters and account/folder expiration dates
detail: Admins can restrict uploadable/shareable file types and set account and file/folder expiration dates. Two otherwise identical users can therefore have different upload capabilities and different access lifetimes. Expiration-driven deprovisioning is a user-state transition worth comparing (active vs expired account responses).
evidence: kiteworks.com Internal Messaging Doc: 'file type filtering feature allows a customer to restrict the types of files that can be uploaded or shared... set account and file/folder expiration dates to ensure that access is only granted for a limited time.'

title: 'Shared with me' view: same user sees different content based on share grants
detail: Users access others' files via a 'Shared with me' navigation pane; individual files can be shared without granting folder access. Two users of identical role therefore see different file sets purely from share grants — the authorization decision is per-object share, not per-role. Useful baseline for owner-vs-nonowner differential work (agent #33).
evidence: Kiteworks Getting Started Guide: 'You can share individual files in a folder without giving users access to other files in the folder. Once shared, users can click the "Shared with me" link in the navigation pane to see files that were shared with them.'

title: System Admin vs Application Admin vs End User: separate API namespaces
detail: Kiteworks REST docs (/rest/index.html) expose distinct endpoint families per role tier: /adminRoles requires authentication with administrative users and only system administrators can elevate users to system/application administrators; regular users cannot promote themselves. /profiles/ exposes per-user privilege/feature templates managed by admins. /roles exposes directory roles. This implies at least three tiers: system administrator (server-wide config, role assignment), application administrator (delegated admin scope), end user (profile-constrained features).
evidence: Kiteworks admin guide PDF mirror (watoniworawi.weebly.com, from Kiteworks admin guide): 'To use adminRoles API your application will need to authenticate with administrative users... only system administrators can [elevate] users to [be] administrators of the system, application administrators. Users cannot promote themselves to system administrators.' /profiles/ 'allows your application to manage the privileges assigned to kiteworks users'; /roles 'get details about directory roles'.

title: End-user file sharing roles: Owner/Manager/Collaborator/Viewer with Details tab audit
detail: Docs show a separate, finer-grained role model at folder/file level for end users: shared folders carry Owner, Manager, Collaborator privileges; shared single files carry Collaborator (edit, download, send) vs Viewer (limited) roles. The assignable set is controlled by the administrator ('Your Kiteworks administrator determines which roles you can assign'). End users with Owner/Manager/Collaborator on a folder see a Details tab with exportable timestamped log of every view/download/upload/rename plus invitation/permission changes — a read surface guests/viewers do not get.
evidence: Kiteworks Getting Started Guide (sca.gdit.com mirror): share-file page on Collaborator vs Viewer roles; 'Shared with me' navigation link. Licensing/Packaging doc (kiteworks.com): 'When end users view a shared folder where they have Owner, Manager, or Collaborator privileges, they can click the Details tab to see an exportable, timestamped log of every user who viewed, downloaded, uploaded, changed, or renamed any file in the folder, as well as changes to user invitations and permissions.'

title: Admin Console vs web app: admins see all user+admin activity; end users see only their own shared-folder activity
detail: Kiteworks architecture white paper distinguishes the two UI surfaces: administrators view ALL end-user AND administrator activity through the Admin Console on the Kiteworks server and can export activity logs to external syslog; end users only see activity through the web app for folders shared with them (uploads, downloads, deletions, comments, tasks), and per-folder activity logs scoped to that folder. So identical underlying events are rendered through a system-wide admin surface vs a per-folder user surface.
evidence: Kiteworks Security Architecture white paper (kiteworks.com): 'Administrators view all end user and administrator activity through the Admin Console on the Kiteworks server. They can also export activity logs to an external syslog server. End users view activity through the Kiteworks web application, such as file uploads, downloads, deletions, comments, and tasks for folders that have been shared with them.'

title: Least-privilege default: users have no privileges until profile assignment; data access only by invitation
detail: Kiteworks Defence Standard guide states the principle of least privilege: all users initially have NO privileges, receiving privileges for functionality only when assigned a user profile, and for data access only by invitation from data managers. Delegated admin roles support configurable per-component permissions. This means a role-vs-role comparison must test two independent axes: (1) profile-driven feature enablement (functionality) and (2) invitation-driven data access.
evidence: Kiteworks guide to Defence Standard (kiteworks.com): 'The Principle of Least Privilege ensures all users initially have no privileges, receiving privileges for functionality only when assigned a user profile and for data access only by invitation from data managers. Delegated admin roles with configurable component scope support admin role CRUD operations.'

title: Restricted users: invited external/guest accounts get restricted profile (SEC deployment example)
detail: SEC's published Kiteworks guide describes the guest/restricted tier: an external recipient is prompted to create an account and is 'by default configured as a restricted user', with account validity tied to the invitation (120 days to that SEC staff member in that deployment). Guests in this model can send/receive with the inviting party but do not get a general-purpose account — differing from full end users who have personal folders and contacts.
evidence: SEC KiteWorks guide (sec.gov): 'You will need to create an account, and by default you will be configured as a restricted user. The account will enable you to send and receive information securely for 120 days to that SEC staff member.'

title: Admin-only API surface: ldapGroups management, device remote-wipe, syslog/export reporting
detail: Docs partition several API groups as administrator-only: /ldapGroups endpoints let admins manage which LDAP groups are available to end users when sharing; /devices exposes per-device access monitoring and remote deletion of any device; admin reporting includes system-level activity logs, built-in/custom reports, compliance dashboards (GDPR/HIPAA). Regular end-user API scope is file/mail/folder operations under their own profile. A useful role-vs-role differential: the same API families (e.g. device list, user search) may return wider fields or extra endpoints for admin callers.
evidence: Kiteworks admin guide mirror: ldapGroups 'administrators can allow LDAP groups to be available to end users when sharing'; devices 'perform remote deletion on any device'. NCA DCC guide (kiteworks.com): 'Administrators have access to extensive reporting capabilities, including system-level activity logs, built-in and custom reports, and compliance-specific dashboards.'

title: Folder role ladder: licensed vs non-licensed roles
detail: Kiteworks folders have a six-role ladder: Owner, Manager, Collaborator (licensed roles, able to edit/download/upload/manage all files in at least one folder) vs Downloader, Uploader, Viewer (non-licensed external roles limited to view/download/upload). Owner is the top role: the content owner determines who gets access and can revoke it (DAC model). A broken owner-check would manifest anywhere a Downloader/Uploader/Viewer performs a Collaborator+ action (edit/manage all files).
evidence: kiteworks.com Licensing and Packaging doc (8.0): 'Licensed Users: ... External Users who have privileges to at least edit, download, upload, and manage all files in at least one folder (Collaborator, Manager, and Owner folder roles)'; 'Nonlicensed Users: External Users who can only view, download, or upload' (Downloader/Uploader/Viewer). kiteworks.com Secure File Sharing with Access Control page: content owner determines who should have access and can revoke it.

title: Only Owners and Managers can manage folder users/roles
detail: Folder collaboration management is restricted to Owners and Managers: they can add/remove users and assign roles in their secure folders (API: POST /rest/folders/{id}/members with userId+roleId payload). Collaborator, Downloader, Uploader, Viewer cannot manage membership. A broken owner-check would be visible as a non-owner successfully calling the members endpoint to add/change roles.
evidence: Accellion/Kiteworks blog (github.com/michael-yee/blogs): 'Collaboration: Folder Owners and Managers can manage users and internal and external stakeholders who have access permissions to their secure folders by assigning them user roles'. Accellion user guide (cdn-cms.f-static.net): POST /rest/folders/{id}/members documented for adding a contact with roleId; GET /rest/roles enumerates roles (downloader role id _2).

title: Activity log visibility differs by role: Details tab only for Owner/Manager/Collaborator
detail: Folder activity tracking (who viewed/downloaded/uploaded/edited/deleted files, added comments, changed invitations/permissions) is exposed via the Details tab ONLY to users holding Owner, Manager, or Collaborator privileges on a shared folder. Downloaders, Uploaders, Viewers must NOT see it. A broken owner-check would be visible as a non-privileged user retrieving the folder activity/tracking log.
evidence: Kiteworks Licensing and Packaging doc (8.0): 'When end users view a shared folder where they have Owner, Manager, or Collaborator privileges, they can click the Details tab to see an exportable, timestamped log of every user who viewed, downloaded, uploaded, changed, or renamed any file in the folder, as well as changes to user invitations and permissions.'

title: Secure link generation restricted to Owner/Manager/Collaborator
detail: Only Folder Owners, Managers, and Collaborators can send recipients a secure link to files. Viewers/Downloaders/Uploaders cannot generate secure links. A broken owner-check would be visible as a lower role obtaining a shareable secure link for content they only view.
evidence: Accellion/Kiteworks blog: 'Secure Links: Folder Owners, Managers, and Collaborators can share files securely by sending recipients a secure link to their files.'

title: Desktop sync enable/disable is Manager-only; notification subscription excludes Viewer/Uploader
detail: Within folders, only users with Manager privileges can enable or disable desktop client sync for individual folders. For email notifications on folder activity: Owners, Managers, Collaborators, and Downloaders can subscribe; Viewers and Uploaders cannot. A broken check would appear as a non-Manager toggling sync or a Viewer/Uploader receiving notification subscriptions.
evidence: Accellion/Kiteworks blog: 'Once folder sync has been enabled, users with Manager privileges can enable or disable sync for individual folders' and 'Notifications: Folder Owners, Managers, Collaborators, and Downloaders can subscribe to receive e-mail alerts'.

title: Online Viewer role: view in browser without download permission
detail: The Viewer role is explicitly defined as view-only via Online Viewer (browser/mobile) WITHOUT permission to download, deliberately avoiding local copies on endpoints. A broken owner-check would be visible as a Viewer obtaining a direct file download (not just rendered view) of a shared file.
evidence: Accellion/Kiteworks blog: 'Online Viewer: Viewers can view documents within the browser or Mobile App without being granted permission to download them. This feature increases not only user productivity but also data security since it does not store local copies of documents on endpoints.'

title: Per-file share roles: Collaborator vs Viewer; shared-with-me list is non-owner view
detail: When sharing an individual file without granting folder access, the owner assigns either Collaborator (permissions to edit, download, send the file, and more) or Viewer (limited permissions); the assignable roles are set by the admin. Non-owners see such files under 'Shared with me'. The owner/non-owner boundary is visible per-file rather than per-folder here: the owner retains the file; the recipient's capabilities are strictly role-bounded.
evidence: Kiteworks Getting Started Guide (multiple mirrors): 'You can share individual files in a folder without giving users access to other files in the folder. Once shared, users can click the Shared with me link... When you share a file, you can assign users the Collaborator role with permissions to edit, download, send the file, and more. Or you can assign them the Viewer role with limited permissions to work with the file. Your Kiteworks administrator determines which roles you can assign.'

title: Email package sender can Track recipients; recipients cannot
detail: For sent email packages, only the sender (owner) can click Track to see a table of which recipients opened the email, viewed attachments, or downloaded them, plus an exportable audit report with timestamps. A recipient cannot access the Track view of a package they received. A broken owner-check would be visible as a non-sender retrieving the tracking report on someone else's package.
evidence: Kiteworks Licensing and Packaging doc (8.0): 'When end users view their sent mail in the Kiteworks web interface, Outlook Plugin, or mobile app, they can click a Track button to see a table showing which recipients have opened the email, viewed the attachments, or downloaded them. A detailed report gives them an exportable audit trail including timestamps.'

title: Historical precedent: role-management input validation bug (CVE-2025-53939, fixed 9.1.0)
detail: CVE-2025-53939: prior to version 9.1.0, improper input validation when managing roles of a shared folder could unexpectedly elevate another user's permissions on the share. This documents the exact model seam where a broken owner-check lives: the roleId/userId handling on the folder members management surface. The target environment is reported at 9.5.1 (all known vulns addressed), so this is evidence of the bug CLASS and location, not a live claim.
evidence: OpenCVE record CVE-2025-53939: 'improper input validation when managing roles of a shared folder could lead to unexpectedly elevate another user's permissions on the share. This issue has been patched in version 9.1.0.'

title: Gap: Kiteworks Secure Data Forms / Advanced Forms owner-vs-submitter model thin in public docs
detail: Public documentation found does not detail the Kiteworks-specific form ownership model (who the 'form owner' is vs form submitters/reviewers, who can read/export submissions, who can edit the form). Generic web-form best-practice docs only advise role-based access on who can modify/view forms and least-privilege access to entered data. This seam is unmapped and may need product docs or in-app inspection, not public search.
evidence: kiteworks.com 'How to Secure Web :Forms' best-practices checklist: 'Deploy Advanced Mechanisms... RBAC... who can modify or view forms' and 'Data... accessible only to individuals who absolutely need it (PoLP)'. No Kiteworks-specific form-owner documentation located.

title: Checklist of visible seams where a broken owner-check would appear
detail: Based on the documented model, a broken owner-check in Kiteworks would be visible at: (1) POST /rest/folders/{id}/members succeeding for a non-Owner/non-Manager caller; (2) folder Details/activity log returned to Downloader/Uploader/Viewer; (3) secure link creation by a Viewer/Downloader; (4) Viewer obtaining a direct download (not Online Viewer render); (5) Downloader uploading/editing files (Collaborator+ only); (6) email recipient accessing Track report on a received package; (7) non-Manager toggling folder desktop sync. These are OBSERVABLE DIFFERENCES, not vulnerability claims.
evidence: Synthesized from the owner-vs-non-owner model recorded in this batch; each seam sourced from the evidence above.

title: SafeEDIT session model: file lock during streaming edit, new version on session end
detail: Documented behavioral model for Kiteworks DRM SafeEDIT (possession-less editing via streaming): every SafeEDIT session is governed end-to-end with 'file locking to prevent conflicting edits'. The session holds a lock while an external user edits in the native application (Word/AutoCAD/Photoshop etc.) via stream; access revocation mid-session ends the session immediately. When the session ends, the edited version is saved automatically as a new version in the Kiteworks repository. Original files stay in the owner's environment throughout. This is a lock-then-version-on-commit model, documented by the vendor — NOT a vulnerability claim.
evidence: https://www.kiteworks.com/platform/digital-rights-management-drm/ : 'comprehensive audit logging of every user action ... and file locking to prevent conflicting edits' ... 'When the session ends, the edited version is saved automatically as a new version in your Kiteworks repository.'

title: Folder-level governance includes admin-controlled locking and versioning
detail: Vendor capability brief documents that admins control 'folder structure, access, permissions, expiration, locking, and versioning' at the folder level, with tracking and versioning to 'make collaboration more effective'. A Kiteworks thought-leadership article frames the documented concurrency stance generally: 'File locking can prevent conflicts but create bottlenecks' and 'Tracking changes during concurrent edits requires sophisticated detection and resolution' — note this article is editorial guidance, not a product behavior spec. Observed model: locking and versioning are governance toggles, not per-edit merge machinery.
evidence: https://www.KiteWorks.com/sites/default/files/resources/kiteworks-capability-brief-file-Sharing.pdf ('Control folder structure, access, permissions, expiration, locking, and versioning'); https://www.kiteworks.com/secure-file-sharing/version-control-security/ (editorial: 'Merge conflicts arise when multiple users edit the same sections simultaneously. File locking can prevent conflicts but create bottlenecks.')

title: Same-name upload creates a new file version (documented API semantics)
detail: Publicly circulated copy of the Kiteworks admin/API guide documents chunk-upload workflow semantics: POST /folders/{id}/actions/initiateUpload starts an upload of a new file, POST /files/{file_id}/actions/initiateUpload starts a new version upload of an existing file, and calling the folder endpoint 'with the file name already exists in this folder, a new version of this file will be created'. Conflict semantics implied: last-writer creates a new version (no merge, no optimistic-concurrency token described). Source caveat: third-party hosted PDF copy of the guide (weebly), not kiteworks.com — treat as lead-grade, not confirmed.
evidence: https://watoniworawi.weebly.com/uploads/1/3/4/8/134871767/33b2bad3c59fc.pdf (Kiteworks admin guide copy): 'If you call POST /folders/{id}/actions/initiateUpload with the file name already exists in this folder, a new version of this file will be created.'

title: File entity carries a 'locked' flag in documented API feedback
detail: The admin guide's documented example API response for file upload feedback includes a 'locked: false' boolean among file metadata fields (description, delete, fingerprint, modified, name, expire, mime, permDeleted, parentId, id, size). This indicates a lock state is tracked per file entity in the backend model, consistent with the SafeEDIT/documented locking behavior. No public documentation found for how the lock is acquired/released via UI or API, or what operations a lock blocks.
evidence: https://watoniworawi.weebly.com/uploads/1/3/4/8/134871767/33b2bad3c59fc.pdf example feedback: { locked: false, description: create: 2020-05-15T06:25:16Z, delete: false, ... id: 1240, size: 2048 }

title: No public doc evidence of optimistic concurrency tokens or merge UI
detail: Across vendor pages, capability briefs, and user guides reviewed, no documentation was found describing optimistic locking (ETag/If-Match style version tokens on edit), three-way merge, or interactive conflict-resolution UI in Kiteworks Core file workflows. The documented strategy appears to be: lock during governed editing sessions (SafeEDIT), version-on-write for uploads, and audit-log everything — i.e., prevention by locking + preservation by versioning, not detection-and-merge. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; API/behavioral verification remains open work. NO race-condition or vulnerability claim is made or implied.
evidence: Negative finding across: kiteworks.com DRM page, file-sharing capability brief, version-control explainer article, Kiteworks Getting Started Guide (kiteworks.sauder.com / sca.gdit.com), SEC Kiteworks user guide (sec.gov)

title: OAuth authorize endpoint exposes a mobile-only auth page variant (m=1 parameter)
detail: Kiteworks API Guide documents that /oauth/authorize accepts an 'm' parameter set to 1 to display a mobile-friendly authorization page. Web and mobile clients authenticate against the same OAuth 2.0 authorization-code endpoint but receive different login/authorization page rendering by a documented parameter, not separate endpoints.
evidence: Accellion/Kiteworks API Guide (kiteworks.com, crawled ~23h ago): 'm (optional parameter) - set to 1 to display mobile friendly authorization page.' Example GET https://kiteworks_server/oauth/authorize?client_id=...&response_type=code&scope=&redirect_uri=...

title: Mobile client keeps files in an AES-256 encrypted on-device secure container with remote wipe; web client does not
detail: The official Kiteworks mobile app datasheet lists a 'Secure container with AES 256 encryption and remote wipe' and states photos taken in-app stay segregated in the app's secure container even when offline. This is a client-side enforcement and storage model that the browser-based web client does not provide (web files live in browser storage/cache, no remote wipe of the browser by the Kiteworks admin).
evidence: Accellion kiteworks Mobile App datasheet (kiteworks.com PDF): 'Secure container with AES 256 encryption and remote wipe' / 'Even when offline, photos are segregated in the app's secure container.'

title: Mobile has offline-access and Express Secure Photo flows not present in the web client
detail: Mobile datasheet lists 'File offline access - user pull and manager push' (admins can push files to devices) and 'Express Secure Photo' (camera capture straight into the secure container). The web client cannot capture photos directly or pre-position offline files on user devices in the same way.
evidence: Kiteworks mobile app datasheet (kiteworks.com): 'File offline access - user pull and manager push' / 'Express Secure Photo'

title: Mobile adds Open-In to whitelisted helper apps plus admin whitelisting of third-party apps
detail: Mobile client supports 'Open-In to edit in any whitelisted app' with 'Admin whitelisting of helper applications' and whitelisting of third-party apps. This makes the mobile client a file-export channel into other apps (controlled by admin allowlist) - a distinct surface from the web client, which edits in-browser or via WOPI without an Open-In handoff to native apps.
evidence: Kiteworks mobile app datasheet: 'Open-In to edit in any whitelisted app' / 'Admin whitelisting of helper applications'; accellion.com mobile app page: 'Whitelisting of third party apps'

title: Mobile and web share the same REST API; the interactive API reference and Playground are browser-only
detail: Developer docs place the single REST API at https://<instance>/rest/index.html and the API Playground as a browser tool - both mobile app and web client are OAuth clients of the same backend endpoints, so no separate mobile API base path is documented. Mobile apps are described as registered OAuth custom applications (client_id/secret/scopes) per the developer portal's prerequisites.
evidence: developer.kiteworks.com: 'The interactive API reference is available at https://<instance>/rest/index.html'; 'Every API integration requires a registered custom application in your Kiteworks Admin console'; kiteworks.com: 'API Playground - Explore live, runnable examples in the browser'

title: Mobile document editing is described via the Microsoft WOPI protocol on iOS - a platform-specific editing path
detail: The mobile datasheet calls out 'Seamless iOS editing in Microsoft Office (Microsoft WOPI protocol)' and a built-in viewer for Office/PDF/images/videos, plus PDF annotation with embedded tools. The web client's Office editing path is not documented the same way in these materials; the mobile app's iOS WOPI integration is its documented editing surface.
evidence: Kiteworks mobile app datasheet: 'Seamless iOS editing in Microsoft Office (Microsoft WOPI protocol)'; accellion.com mobile page: 'Annotate PDFs using embedded annotation tools' / 'Preview over 200 types of files securely without having to download them'

title: Mobile auth options documented include RADIUS 2FA/MFA and native OTP-based 2FA
detail: The mobile datasheet lists 'RADIUS 2FA/MFA, native OTP based 2FA, OAUTH' as the mobile security stack. The Getting Started Guide describes generic web 2FA (emailed/text passcodes or authenticator app, plus 'Remember this device' trusted-device option). Mobile explicitly ties RADIUS-based 2FA/MFA and native OTP 2FA to the mobile client, a narrower auth-option set than the web's password/passcode/RSA/YubiKey/certificate-based options.
evidence: Kiteworks mobile app datasheet: 'RADIUS 2FA/MFA, native OTP based 2FA, OAUTH'; Getting Started Guide: 'For example, a passcode may be emailed to your account, or other credentials using mechanisms such as RSA token or YubiKey may be required' / 'Sign in using certificate based authentication'

title: Kiteworks operates staging.kiteworks.com (publicly indexed staging web tier)
detail: A publicly indexed Kiteworks staging host exists: staging.kiteworks.com, which hosts Kiteworks resource PDFs (e.g. the 'Secure Data Forms hardening' solution brief, crawled ~120 days ago). This shows Kiteworks uses a staging tier for its web content infrastructure. It is NOT a bounty product host and is NOT in scope; recorded only as evidence Kiteworks maintains staging-tier hosts.
evidence: browser.search result 4 (2026-09-27): 'SOLUTION BRIEF†staging.kiteworks.com' with URL https://staging.kiteworks.com/sites/default/files/resources/kiteworks-brief-secure-data-forms-hardening-solution.pdf, last crawled ~120 days ago.

title: Program page refers to 'hunting environments' (plural) but lists only one in-scope URL
detail: The YesWeHack Kiteworks program page says 'we monitor all activities on our hunting environments' (plural), yet the 'Kiteworks Access' section lists exactly one URL: https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev. No staging-vs-prod pair is advertised to public researchers; other hunting environments (if any) are not documented on the public program page.
evidence: https://yeswehack.com/programs/kiteworks-public-bug-bounty-program-1 — 'Monitoring of our hunting environments' section vs 'Kiteworks Access: KW Access: https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev' (single entry).

title: Documented version delta: hunting-env build exposes numeric user IDs; 'next release' moves to UUID
detail: The program page's Known Issues/Accepted risks section documents the current build's behavior vs a future build: 'Listing internal users by ID. Only restricted users and recipient should not be able to send a message to other users. (ID will be replaced by UUID in the next release.)' The hunting environment therefore runs a build with sequential/numeric user identifiers; a subsequent release changes the identifier scheme to UUID.
evidence: https://yeswehack.com/programs/kiteworks-public-bug-bounty-program-1 — Known Issues/Accepted risks bullet: 'ID will be replaced by UUID in the next release.'

title: Version boundary: 9.1.0 fixed role-management input validation (CVE-2025-53939); 9.5.1 is the current known-good build
detail: Public records document at least two build boundaries on Kiteworks Core: CVE-2025-53939 (improper input validation when managing roles of a shared folder, could elevate another user's permissions) was patched in 9.1.0; Kiteworks' Sep 26 2026 advisory states 9.5.1 accounts for all known vulnerabilities. The hunting environment is associated with the 9.5.1 build; older builds differ on the folder role-management surface.
evidence: OpenCVE CVE-2025-53939 (patched in 9.1.0). Kiteworks press release 'Kiteworks Precautionary Shutdown Advisory for Customers' (kiteworks.com, Sep 2026): 'Kiteworks has accounted for all known vulnerabilities in our current release, 9.5.1.'

title: Architecture delta: Secure Data Forms rearchitected form-data storage vs 123FormBuilder (CVE-2026-24782, 9.4 -> 7.6)
detail: Kiteworks' own Secure Data Forms hardening brief documents a generational architecture difference: SQL injection vectors identified in CVE-2026-24782 in the 123FormBuilder architecture score 9.4, but the same vectors against Kiteworks Secure Data Forms score 7.6 because engineers 'rearchitected how SDF stores submitted form data' placing it outside reach of those SQLi vectors. SDF also runs in a dedicated single-tenant environment per customer vs 123FormBuilder's shared multi-tenant SaaS. This is documented as a product-generation difference, not a staging-vs-prod difference.
evidence: Kiteworks 'Secure Data Forms hardening' solution brief (hosted on staging.kiteworks.com): 'the SQL injection vectors identified in CVE-2026-24782... contributed meaningfully to the drop from 9.4 to 7.6'; 'Kiteworks Secure Data Forms runs in a dedicated singletenant environment for each customer' vs '123FormBuilder, which operates as a shared SaaS platform.'

title: Single-tenant deployment model: no shared staging tenant concept in Kiteworks Core
detail: The program page states 'Kiteworks is deployed single-tenant and operated by each customer's own administrators. A corporate administrator already has effective control of the underlying appliance.' This documents that Kiteworks Core has no shared multi-tenant staging tier where cross-tenant leakage would apply — each deployment is its own production-like hardened appliance instance.
evidence: https://yeswehack.com/programs/kiteworks-public-bug-bounty-program-1 — 'Important information about vulnerabilities that require admin privileges' section.

title: Hunting environment is a hardened appliance deployment, not a reduced staging tier
detail: The program describes the Kiteworks ecosystem as four logical environments (Core Node, EPG, Advanced Forms, MFT), each 'on a hardened Kiteworks appliance', and the $25k bonus rules require 'root access ... on the underlying hardened appliance itself — root access limited to a single container does not qualify'. This documents the hunting environment as a full hardened-appliance deployment (Core node), not a trimmed staging replica.
evidence: https://yeswehack.com/programs/kiteworks-public-bug-bounty-program-1 — 'Kiteworks ecosystem' section (4 environments on hardened appliances) and bonus notes: 'Root access must be achieved on the underlying hardened appliance itself—root access limited to a single container does not qualify.'

title: Kiteworks ships a documented nonproduction/test concept (API Playground / trial systems)
detail: The Kiteworks admin guide documents that trial systems and the API Playground are nonproduction: 'Within minutes of signing up, your Trial Accellion system in the cloud will be ready to use... This test is not intended for commercial purposes in the production environment, its sole purpose is to develop and test nonproduction.' Trial systems are provisioned per-signup and expired (not persistent). This shows the vendor's own dev/test-vs-prod separation is per-instance trial systems, not a shared public staging product environment.
evidence: Kiteworks admin guide mirror (watoniworawi.weebly.com, from Kiteworks admin guide PDF): 'This test is not intended for commercial purposes in the production environment, its sole purpose is to develop and test nonproduction.'

title: Certificate-transparency query for *.bounty.kiteworks.dev inconclusive (crt.sh unreachable)
detail: Two attempts to query crt.sh for certificates under %.bounty.kiteworks.dev (a passive public source for staging/dev subdomain references) failed: empty response and HTTP 000 from this network. No certificate-log evidence for a staging/dev sibling of the hunting environment was retrieved; this is a tool failure, NOT evidence that no such host exists.
evidence: curl to https://crt.sh/?q=%25.bounty.kiteworks.dev&output=json on 2026-09-27: first attempt returned unparseable empty body; retry returned http:000 size:0.

title: Origin unreachable from this egress: all 8 timing probes timed out
detail: Measured response times for GET / , /robots.txt, /.well-known/security.txt, and one nonexistent path (2 requests each, ~3s apart, UA containing '-public-yeswehack', --max-time 20s). Every request returned HTTP code 000 with connect time 0.000s and total time pinned at ~20.0s (the client timeout). No response was received for any path, so no path-to-path timing differential could be measured. The environment egresses via an HTTP proxy; the proxy-to-origin connection to ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev:443 timed out on all attempts. This is an infrastructure/path-reachability fact, not an origin-behavior fact.
evidence: curl -w timing runs on 2026-09-27: 8/8 requests -> code 000, total=20.003-20.007s, connect=0.000s; direct + proxied attempts both failed at connect

title: No timing baseline obtainable; recommend retry timing measurements via browser-task route
detail: Since no TCP connection to the origin completed from this agent's network path, repeat measurements from a vantage point with working egress (parent-agent browser task with timing instrumentation, or a sanctioned researcher network) are needed before any path/parameter timing comparison. No timing differences were observed; none could be observed.
evidence: complete absence of successful responses in 8 attempts across 4 public paths

title: GET/HEAD/OPTIONS comparison not executable: target unreachable from swarm sandbox
detail: All direct requests to https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev (paths /, /robots.txt, /.well-known/security.txt; methods GET/HEAD/OPTIONS) timed out with HTTP 000. 8 requests attempted total, UA 'Deephunt-Swarm35-public-yeswehack'. No status codes, Allow headers, or body differences could be recorded because no response was ever received.

No proxy refusal code; the tunnel simply never establishes. 8 requests total, all seconds+ apart, all within the <=10 budget.

title: Sandbox egress path cannot distinguish host-down vs proxy-block for this target
detail: The CONNECT timeout gives no signal about the target's actual state: the world model records HTTP 200 on / from earlier work, so the host is presumably up; from this sandbox it is not reachable. Method-comparison work from this environment must be re-run from a network that can reach the host, or skipped.
evidence: Same curl session output as above: proxy CONNECT negotiation succeeds ('Connected to hatch-egress-proxy', 'Proxy auth using Basic'), then silence until timeout. No RST, no 403/407/502 from the proxy.

title: 9.3.0 vs 9.2.x: Secure Data Forms added ownership checks on form resources (IDORs removed)
detail: Pre-9.3.0 Secure Data Forms endpoints allowed an authenticated user to tamper with other users' form approval-flow configs, modify other users' form resources, modify other users' resource permissions, and read other users' resource metadata — cross-user object operations succeeded. From 9.3.0 these same operations must enforce resource-ownership checks; requests that previously succeeded should now be rejected. This is a behavioral delta on the Forms API surface between 9.2.x and 9.3.0.
evidence: OpenCVE Kiteworks list: CVE-2026-23638 (approval-flow tamper), CVE-2026-24753/24756 (modify others' resources), CVE-2026-24755 (modify others' permissions), CVE-2026-24761 (read others' metadata) — all 'Prior to version 9.3.0 ... Upgrade Kiteworks to version 9.3.0 or later'.

title: 9.3.0 vs 9.2.x: Secure Data Forms input neutralization changed (stored+reflected XSS closed)
detail: Pre-9.3.0 Secure Data Forms rendered unencoded user input into pages for both stored XSS (authenticated attacker, incl. when modifying forms) and reflected XSS (external attacker tricking a user). From 9.3.0 output encoding/neutralization must differ: previously-executing payloads in form views should now render inert. This changes how form fields are echoed in the UI between 9.2.x and 9.3.0.
evidence: OpenCVE Kiteworks list: CVE-2026-24751/24752 (reflected XSS, 8.2 High), CVE-2026-24754 (stored XSS, 5.4), CVE-2026-24750 (stored XSS via form modification, pre-9.2.1/9.3.0) — all patched by upgrading past the named versions.

title: 9.3.0 vs 9.2.x: Secure Data Forms FormBuilder input handling changed (SQL injection removed)
detail: Pre-9.3.0, a FormBuilder-role user could exploit multiple SQL injection points to retrieve or modify other users' form definitions and some global configuration parameters. From 9.3.0 parameterized input handling must replace the old behavior; error/behavior of form-definition queries with hostile input should change between 9.2.x and 9.3.0.
evidence: OpenCVE Kiteworks list: CVE-2026-24782 (7.6 High): 'Prior to version 9.3.0, multiple SQL Injection vulnerabilities in Kiteworks Secure Data Forms ... Upgrade Kiteworks to version 9.3.0 or later to receive a patch'.

title: 9.2.0 vs 9.1.x: configuration layer added SSRF DNS-rebinding protection and upload validation
detail: Pre-9.2.0 the configuration functionality allowed bypassing SSRF protections via DNS rebinding, and the configuration upload path accepted arbitrary files without proper validation. From 9.2.0 both behaviors changed: SSRF protections must now tolerate/deny rebinding tricks, and config uploads must validate file types. Admin-facing config endpoints behave differently pre- vs post-9.2.0.
evidence: OpenCVE Kiteworks list: CVE-2026-28271 (SSRF bypass via DNS rebinding, patched in 9.2.0), CVE-2026-28270 (config file upload without proper validation, patched in 9.2.0).

title: 9.2.0 vs 9.1.x: command execution output redirection restricted
detail: Pre-9.2.0, authenticated users could redirect command execution output to arbitrary file locations (overwrite critical system files / elevate). From 9.2.0 output destinations must be constrained; commands that previously wrote anywhere should now fail or be confined. Behavioral delta in the command-execution path at the 9.2.0 boundary.
evidence: OpenCVE Kiteworks list: CVE-2026-28269 (5.9 Medium): 'Prior to version 9.2.0 ... allows authenticated users to redirect command output to arbitrary file locations. ... Version 9.2.0 contains a patch'.

title: 9.2.1 vs 9.2.0: Core access-control tightened; EPG disabled-account sessions revoked; Forms credential-transport/upload fixed
detail: Kiteworks Core 9.2.0/9.2.1 let authenticated users access unauthorized content (fixed 9.2.2). Email Protection Gateway let blocked users keep active sessions after account disable (pre-9.2.1). Secure Data Forms pre-9.2.1 had credential-transport misconfigurations and a manager-side unrestricted dangerous-file upload. All of these are old-vs-new behavior boundaries: 9.2.2 Core must deny previously-allowed content access; 9.2.1 EPG must kill blocked-user sessions; Forms must validate uploads and protect credential transport.
evidence: OpenCVE Kiteworks list: CVE-2026-23514 (Core 8.8 High, fixed 9.2.2), CVE-2026-29092 (EPG blocked-user session, fixed 9.2.1), CVE-2026-23635 (credentials transport, fixed 9.2.1), CVE-2026-23636 (unrestricted upload, fixed 9.2.1).

title: 9.1.0 vs 9.0.x: shared-folder role management input validation added; MFT Connections role/permission model tightened
detail: Pre-9.1.0, improper input validation when managing roles of a shared folder could unexpectedly elevate another user's share permissions; separately, MFT Connections management had an unfavorable role/permission definition allowing unexpected privilege escalation by authorized users. From 9.1.0 both paths must validate/enforce differently: previously-elevating role changes should now be refused or constrained.
evidence: OpenCVE Kiteworks list: CVE-2025-53939 (shared-folder role input validation, patched 9.1.0), CVE-2025-53900 (MFT Connections roles/permissions, patched 9.1.0).

title: 9.4 vs 9.3: Secure MFT Server added a standards-interoperable AS2 trading-partner surface
detail: Kiteworks Secure MFT Server v9.4 earned Drummond AS2 certification (AS2-2Q26 and AS2-4Q25 test events), validating send/receive of AS2 messages with payload integrity, digital signatures, encryption, and sync/async MDN receipts, plus structured MDN error statuses on corrupted messages. AS2 B2B message exchange behavior (message structure, signature/encryption negotiation, receipt handling, error signaling) is a NEW externally-reachable protocol surface versus earlier versions.
evidence: Kiteworks press release 2026-06-18 (einnews.com): 'Kiteworks Secure MFT Server v9.4 is listed by Drummond Group as an AS2 certified product for the AS2-2Q26 and AS2-4Q25 interoperability test events'; Drummond tested corrupted-message error handling requiring appropriate MDN error statuses.

title: 7.7-7.10 era: new admin console, EPG role separation, MFT client auto-update, SHA3-256 fingerprints
detail: Public 'What's Coming' notices show a multi-release migration path relevant to old-vs-new comparisons: 7.7 added a preview new admin console (admins could toggle between new and classic consoles) and DRM-protected attachments; 7.8 enhanced health monitoring and added SAML SP certificate upload; 7.10 brought EPG role/service separation into cluster nodes, multinode EPG database, MFT client auto-update, and SHA3-256 digital fingerprints alongside MD5. Admin UI behavior, EPG deployment topology, and file fingerprint hashes all changed across these releases; the classic/new admin console toggle means two coexisting UIs with potentially different endpoint coverage.
evidence: Kiteworks 7.7/7.8/7.10 What's Coming customer notices (kiteworks.com): 7.7 new admin interface preview + license-release flow changes; 7.8 admin SAML cert upload + health monitoring; 7.10 EPG multinode DB, role separation, MFT client automatic update, SHA3-256 fingerprints.

title: Data gap: no public 9.4.x/9.5.x feature changelog found
detail: Searches across Kiteworks press releases, what's-new notices, and CVE databases surfaced no public feature-level changelog for 9.4 (beyond the AS2 certification), 9.5, or 9.5.1. Version-to-version behavior deltas for the newest releases cannot be mapped from public sources alone; the hunting environment's version string and response behaviors are the only available evidence.
evidence: Four targeted web searches (release notes 9.x, what's-coming 9.x, 8.x-to-9.x migration, 9.5 new features) returned incident coverage and 7.x-era notices only; no 9.4/9.5 feature changelog indexed publicly.

Only 2 of the 10-request budget used. No HTML/JS/URL/email rendering of filenames or display names could be compared on the live site from this network; any prior world-model claims about live headers/content remain unverified from here.

title: Context inventory (docs only): same filename appears in HTML UI, email link, and download contexts
detail: Public Kiteworks user guides (SEC staff guide) document three distinct rendering contexts for a user-supplied filename: (1) web inbox UI ('the Inbox is now displayed', file names listed in browser), (2) notification email ('click on the Attachment link within the email'), (3) download flow after authentication ('Click the Download button to download'). Whether each context encodes the same filename identically (HTML-entity vs URL-encoded vs Content-Disposition header encoding) is UNOBSERVED — listed as candidate contexts for future differential work, not as a difference.

detail: Because no HTTP response was ever received, there is no data on whether Accept/Accept-Language differences change response format, error pages, or localization. This question remains open for an agent with a reachable network path. Nothing here implies a vulnerability or a misconfiguration on the target's side.

title: Core REST API versioning is header-based via X-Accellion-Version, not URL paths
detail: All historical docs and code samples pin behavior with the X-Accellion-Version HTTP header (values 8, 10, 15 seen in examples), while endpoints share the same /rest/... paths. No /v1/ style URL versioning observed anywhere in Kiteworks docs.
evidence: cdn-cms.f-static.net user guide: header_data={'X-Accellion-Version':'8'}; watoniworawi admin guide: X-Accellion-Version: 15 in curl samples; kiteworks.com API guide

title: Current Core API spec is v28; Pub-Sub API is separately tracked at v1
detail: The current Kiteworks Developer Portal publishes two versioned spec families: Core APIs at v28 (files, folders, mail, forms, user management, search) and Pub-Sub APIs at v1 (event streaming / webhook integrations). Version numbers are per-spec-family, not a single global product version.
evidence: developer.kiteworks.com/api-specs.html: 'Core APIs v28 ... Pub-Sub APIs v1 ... Each spec is versioned and available in multiple formats'

title: Version history spans v8 to v28 but no public changelog of what changed between versions was found
detail: Examples in dated docs use EAPI 8 (OAuth flows), 10 (folder listing), 15 (folder creation cURL); current spec is v28. Despite at least 20 version bumps, no published per-version changelog or breaking-change list was found in searched docs; search results only show the current version number, not deltas.
evidence: search results above; developer portal page shows only current v28/v1 with no version history or 'what changed' notes

title: Older docs claim 'several versions of the API, all of which are supported' - no sunset schedule stated
detail: The Accellion-era API guides state that several API versions are all supported and that new versions are periodically introduced to improve security and performance, with a recommendation to use the latest. No deprecation dates, sunset headers, or version-removal policy were found in the docs reviewed.
evidence: kiteworks.com API guide (crawl 23h ago): 'There are several API versions, all of which are supported. To maintain and improve security and performance, Accellion periodically introduces API versions.'

title: OAuth grant-type surface narrowed between old and current docs (7 grant types -> 2 named flows)
detail: The older API guide lists 7 token grant types: Authorization Code, Signature-based Authorization Code, Signature-based Access, User Credential, User Credential (HTTP Basic), SAML 2.0 Assertion, JWT Assertion. The current developer-portal page describes only OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code and JWT Assertion flows, and emphasizes step-by-step OAuth/JWT auth guides. Legacy signature-based and user-credential grants may be version-dependent or deprecated, but no doc found explicitly states that.
evidence: kiteworks.com API guide token grant list vs developer.kiteworks.com secure-integrations page ('Authentication guides walk through OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code and JWT Assertion flows')

title: Old in-product Swagger playground at /rest/index.html coexists with the new OpenAPI developer portal
detail: Older docs direct developers to <host>/rest/index.html (Swagger UI with a 'Get a Token' / version selector and a ?download_token bootstrap) while the modern developer portal serves OpenAPI specs importable into Postman/Insomnia and an interactive API Reference. Whether the hunting environment exposes /rest/index.html and which spec versions it serves there is unmeasured (passive only).
evidence: kiteworks.com API guide: 'enter the kiteworks URL instance/rest/index.html ... Click the API version and select the latest version'; developer.kiteworks.com/api-specs.html and api-reference.html

title: Creation endpoints return X-Accellion-Location response header; returnEntity flag changes response body
detail: 201 Created responses place the new resource URI in the X-Accellion-Location response header; the request flag returnEntity=true also includes the created entity JSON in the response body (seen in folder-creation example). This header pattern appears version-stable across the docs reviewed.
evidence: watoniworawi admin guide cURL example: POST /rest/folders/0/folders?returnEntity=true -> X-Accellion-Location contains URI

title: OAuth scope format uses wildcard path patterns per resource (e.g. */files/* */folders/*)
detail: Docs show requested scopes as space-separated wildcard path patterns such as '*/activities/* */admin/* */profile/* */users/* */files/* */folders/*'. Token response includes token_type bearer, expires_in, and scope echoed in the same pattern format. This pattern-based scoping differs from modern OAuth scope-name conventions and is worth comparing against the hunting environment's token endpoint behavior.
evidence: kiteworks.com API guide Python example and token-response JSON example

title: Nonexistent plain paths render identical branded SPA error page
detail: GET /no-such-path-xyz-404 and GET /a/b/c/nonexistent/deep both return a Kiteworks-branded page reading '# Kiteworks / Error / The link is inaccessible. / Return to sign in' with a 'Return to sign in' link. No path echo, no stack trace, no version leak in extracted text. Error format is uniform regardless of path depth or segment content.
evidence: browser.open fetched https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/no-such-path-xyz-404 and /a/b/c/nonexistent/deep on 2026-09-27; both rendered the same 6-line branded error page

title: /rest/* nonexistent endpoint returns raw HTTP 404, not the branded page
detail: GET /rest/no-such-endpoint-zz was rejected upstream with http_status=404 (raw status, browser could not extract a page). This differs from unknown non-/rest/ paths, which return the branded SPA error page. The /rest prefix appears to bypass the SPA fallback and surface a real 404 status.
evidence: browser.open on https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/rest/no-such-endpoint-zz on 2026-09-27 -> upstream_status=404

title: Encoded-traversal path returns HTTP 400
detail: GET /%2e%2e/%2e%2e/nope-404-test was rejected upstream with http_status=400 (no page content extracted). Encoded dot-segment paths are rejected with 400 rather than falling through to the branded SPA error page, indicating server-side path normalization/validation before routing.
evidence: browser.open on https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/nope-404-test on 2026-09-27 -> upstream_status=400

title: Root path / returns no extractable content via fetch
detail: GET / succeeded at fetch level but had no extractable page text (likely JS-rendered sign-in shell). Unlike nonexistent paths which produce a text-bearing branded error page, the root exposes no error text to a text-only fetcher.
evidence: browser.open on https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/ on 2026-09-27 -> 'page had no extractable content'

title: No verbose errors, stack traces, or version leaks observed in error paths
detail: Across 5 error-path probes (plain 404s, deep path, /rest 404, encoded traversal, root), no response carried a stack trace, framework version string, or debug detail. All differences were in routing behavior (branded page vs raw 404 vs raw 400), not in error verbosity.
evidence: aggregated from all 5 browser.open probes on 2026-09-27 against ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev

title: GET / headers arrive but response body never starts (chunked, no chunks)
detail: HTTPS GET / returns HTTP 200 with full headers (TTFB ~10.2s) and Transfer-Encoding: chunked, but the response body never begins: no bytes arrived within 25s and curl timed out. HEAD / to the same URL returns instantly (~5s incl. proxy). robots.txt and other paths behave the same way on GET (headers arrive, body hangs).
evidence: curl -A 'deephunt-obs-71-public-yeswehack' https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/ -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, TTFB 10.233s, then (28) timeout after 25s with zero body bytes. 2026-09-27 05:37 GMT.

title: Even trivial static responses take 5-16s TTFB
detail: TTFB is enormous for everything, including a 69-byte static robots.txt (6.8s), a 302 redirect for a nonexistent path (16.1s), /login_config (10.4s), and even a failed plain-HTTP connection (11.7s before empty reply). Nothing responds quickly.
evidence: HEAD timings via curl -w time_starttransfer on 2026-09-27: /robots.txt 6.84s, /nonexistent-deephunt-probe-xyz 16.06s, /login_config 10.35s, port-80 / 11.73s.

title: Nonexistent paths return 302 'Moved Temporarily' to /error?status=404, not 404
detail: GET/HEAD on a garbage path does not return 404; it returns '302 Moved Temporarily' with Location: https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/error?status=404 and a 112-byte body. The reason phrase 'Moved Temporarily' is the HTTP/1.0-era wording rather than the modern 'Found'.
evidence: curl -I https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/nonexistent-deephunt-probe-xyz -> 'HTTP/1.1 302 Moved Temporarily' / 'Location: https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/error?status=404' / Content-Length: 112. 2026-09-27.

title: Plain HTTP on port 80: connection killed with empty reply, no redirect to HTTPS
detail: http://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/ on port 80 does not redirect to HTTPS and does not return an error status; after ~11.7s the server closes the connection with zero response bytes (curl: (52) Empty reply from server).
evidence: curl -I http://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/ -> (52) Empty reply from server, ttfb=11.73s. 2026-09-27.

title: Caching headers inconsistent across endpoints
detail: / and /login_config send 'Pragma: no-cache' and 'Expires: 0' plus Cache-Control: no-store..., while /robots.txt (ETag + Last-Modified + Accept-Ranges, Content-Length: 69) and the 302 error redirect carry Cache-Control: no-store but NO Pragma/Expires. A static immutable-looking file (Last-Modified Sep 04 2026, ETag) is still marked no-store.
evidence: HEAD responses 2026-09-27: / and /login_config include Pragma/Expires; /robots.txt and 302 /error?status=404 do not, despite robots.txt having ETag "6a9a88f3-45" / Last-Modified: Fri, 04 Sep 2026 09:01:39 GMT.

title: /login_config answers 200 as application/javascript but declares no body framing
detail: HEAD /login_config returns 200 with Content-Type: application/javascript; charset=UTF-8 but neither Content-Length nor Transfer-Encoding in the HEAD response, unlike / (chunked) and /robots.txt (Content-Length: 69). Its body framing for GET is unobservable because GET bodies never arrive.
evidence: curl -I https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/login_config -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, Content-Type: application/javascript; charset=UTF-8, no Content-Length, no Transfer-Encoding. 2026-09-27.

title: Soft-404 pattern: nonexistent paths return 302 to /error?status=404, never a 404 status
detail: GET /api, /dashboard, /no-such-path-zz91, /.well-known/security.txt all return HTTP 302 with Location: https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/error?status=404 and a 112-byte stock nginx '302 Found' body. The application never emits a 404 status to anonymous visitors; missing-path information is encoded in the redirect query string instead.
evidence:
4/4 nonexistent paths -> 302, Location /error?status=404, 112B body '

302 Found

'. Captured response headers saved per-path.

title: Auth-required redirect is distinguishable from soft-404: /admin/ -> 302 /login?LoginRedir=%2Fadmin
detail: GET /admin/ returns 302 with Location: /login?LoginRedir=%2Fadmin (0-byte body), whereas nonexistent paths 302 to /error?status=404. The two redirect targets have distinct server-side meanings: 'exists but requires authentication' vs 'does not exist'. An anonymous visitor can therefore distinguish protected-but-existing routes from missing ones by the Location value. A LoginRedir return-path parameter is present on the auth redirect.
evidence: GET /admin/ -> 302, Location: https://ywh-kw-public.bounty.kiteworks.dev/login?LoginRedir=%2Fadmin. Contrast /dashboard -> 302 /error?status=404.

title: /admin is the only tested path with trailing-slash normalization (301 -> /admin/)
detail: GET /admin returns 301 Moved Permanently to /admin/ (136B stock nginx body). None of the other tested paths (/api, /dashboard, /login, random) exhibit trailing-slash normalization. This reveals /admin/ is a real directory/route on the server, unlike the soft-404'd paths.
evidence: GET /admin -> 301, Location .../admin/. All other bad paths -> 302 /error?status=404.

title: Zero Set-Cookie headers across all anonymous responses
detail: Across 9 anonymous requests (/, /robots.txt, /.well-known/security.txt, /login, /api, /admin, /admin/, /dashboard, random path), the server set zero cookies. No session, CSRF, or anonymous-tracking cookie is issued pre-authentication on these endpoints.
evidence: grep -c '^set-cookie:' = 0 on all 9 captured header files.

title: / and /login serve byte-identical 200 responses (2346B SPA shell)
detail: GET / and GET /login both return 200 text/html with byte-identical 2346-byte bodies: an HTML shell with empty <title>, meta robots noindex, viewport meta. There is no separate server-rendered login page; the login UI is presumably client-rendered from the same entry point.
evidence: diff b_.txt b_login.txt -> identical. Body starts '<!doctype html><html lang="en"><head><title></title>'.

title: /.well-known/security.txt does NOT serve content (corrects dossier)
detail: The world-model seed lists /.well-known/security.txt as 'exists'. It responds 302 -> /error?status=404 like any missing path. It exists as a URL that was probed, but serves no security.txt content to anonymous visitors.
evidence: GET /.well-known/security.txt -> 302, Location /error?status=404.

title: robots.txt is 'Disallow: /' for all agents; page carries meta noindex
detail: GET /robots.txt -> 200 text/plain 69B: 'User-agent: * / Disallow: /'. The HTML shell also carries <meta name="robots" content="noindex">. The operator disallows all crawling and indexing.
evidence: 69-byte body, quoted verbatim above.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL: total egress HTTPS outage ~10 min during this run; target not at fault
detail: At ~05:35-05:45 UTC all outbound HTTPS from this environment timed out (target, example.com, crt.sh), while DNS resolution worked. After ~3 min idle, connectivity recovered and the target answered 200 in 6.4s. Cause is environmental (likely egress-proxy saturation from many swarm agents issuing concurrent requests), NOT target blocking. Recommendation for the director: stagger direct-request agents; concurrent bursts risk self-inflicted denial of the research channel and could look like aggressive scanning from the target's side.
evidence: curl to 3 hosts x timeout; nslookup OK; retry after 150s idle -> HTTP 200 in 6.389s.
